item.title: Discontinued Cracker Barrel foods that fans are begging to get back
item.description: The Sunrise Sampler breakfast platter and black-eyed peas are among the discontinued comfort foods loyal customers want Cracker Barrel to bring back.
item.content:encoded:
Cracker Barrel Old Country Store has built its reputation on serving Southern comfort food and nostalgic favorites, which may explain why some discontinued menu items continue to spark passionate reactions from loyal customers.

From black-eyed peas and fried haddock to red-eye gravy and fried chicken livers, fans have taken to social media and online forums over the years to call for the return of beloved classics.

One breakfast favorite that still has customers talking is the Sunrise Sampler, a platter that combined eggs, grits, fried apples, hash brown casserole, sausage, bacon, country ham and biscuits with gravy.

CRACKER BARREL COMEBACK GAINS STEAM AS LOYAL CUSTOMER SAYS RETURN VISIT 'FELT LIKE COMING HOME'

"I noticed a while back that Cracker Barrel removed the GOAT of all breakfasts, the Sunrise Sampler, from the menu," Josh Cooper, owner of Cooper's Next Level BBQ in Tallahassee, Florida, told Fox News Digital. "You used to get a little bit of everything without breaking the bank."

Cooper said recreating the same meal today requires ordering each item separately, driving up the cost.

"Now in order to get that same teaser touch from the Sunrise Sampler, you have to order it all à la carte, which costs around $25 for the same great meal," he said. "Blasphemy!"

Fox News Digital reached out to Cracker Barrel for comment.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

While menu changes are often driven by rising ingredient costs or operational challenges, Cooper said restaurants should recognize the emotional attachment customers have to longtime favorites.

"The reality is that nostalgia matters and when you remove popular items without controlling the narrative or managing customers' expectations, you are bound to have upset patrons," he said.

"Whether it's due to rising food costs, kitchen timing or any other reason, it's important to communicate with the people who put you on the map in the first place. Communication matters."

Cracker Barrel faced backlash last summer over efforts to modernize its image, including a short-lived logo redesign and restaurant makeover. Last week, the company announced that CEO Julie Masino would step down.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Rachel Love, a self-described Cracker Barrel enthusiast from Tennessee, said black-eyed peas are a side dish that she hopes will make a return.

"I absolutely loved the black-eyed peas, and I'm so glad they're getting some attention," Love told Fox News Digital. "They were one of my favorite sides and always felt like such a classic part of the Cracker Barrel experience."

She also hopes the chain will revive its baked apple dumpling, which she described as "the perfect comfort dessert" that matched the restaurant's nostalgic atmosphere.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The appeal goes beyond any single dish, Love said.

"People aren't just asking for old menu items — they're asking for the comfort and nostalgia that came with them," she said. 

"Sometimes bringing back one classic dish means more to loyal customers than introducing several new ones."

item.title: Historian blasts Smithsonian's activism shift after first visit in over a decade: 'Completely different place'
item.description: Dr. Jody Edward Ginn says the Smithsonian National Museum of American History abandoned education for activism after visiting for the first time since 2012
item.content:encoded:
A historian and museum professional accused the Smithsonian of abandoning its educational mission in favor of activism following his visit to the National Museum of American History (NMAH) for the first time in more than a decade amid mounting criticism from the Trump administration and conservatives over how the museum presents American history.

"It's a completely different place than when I was there in 2012," Dr. Jody Edward Ginn told Fox News Digital.

"Its mission is clearly exactly what they changed it to be. It is a museum for activism. They use history, but that's kind of the problem. You know, scholars of history, and I don't consider these folks scholars anymore. They're activists."

After reading the administration's Domestic Policy Council report accusing the Smithsonian and the NMAH of failing to present history "in a way that is inspiring, unifying, and worthy of our great republic," Ginn said he traveled all the way from Texas to see it for himself.

INSIDE THE BEHEMOTH SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM NETWORK DRAWING FIRE FROM THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION

"From the moment I walked in, it's a very different experience," Ginn said. "Now, I wasn't totally shocked by this because I've been watching this evolution in my field for over a decade."

As he made his way through the exhibits, Ginn said the institution seeks to "specifically direct" visitors "to action" rather than give them the information to "make their own decisions."

"It became this goal, their own stated goal, to turn museums from institutions of education, of public education, into institutions to encourage activism, which could also be said to indoctrinate."

Ginn said he found "factually incorrect information" in some exhibits but argued what they don't tell visitors is just as misleading.

WATCH: SMITHSONIAN HISTORY MUSEUM DIRECTOR STUMBLES OVER BASIC QUESTIONS ON SEX: ‘I’M NOT SURE’

"The biggest problem is in what they leave out," he said.

Ginn argued the museum's "graphic" and sexually explicit exhibits have no place in a museum frequented by children and families, saying they're "out of sync with what museums were just a few years ago."

"These are geared towards all ages," he said. "Why would you do that? All of that's out of sync with what museums were just a few years ago."

In a House hearing last month, lawmakers raised similar concerns during a House hearing, pressing Smithsonian National Museum of American History Director Anthea Hartig about the museum's exhibits.

Rep. Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., asked Hartig about the exhibit titled "Illegal to Be You: Gay History Beyond Stonewall," which featured a bondage harness, saying "You have pictures of bondage, you have some overtly sexual things up there, you have transgender folks."

Lawmakers also questioned Hartig about the 2017 MASS Action Toolkit, a guide for museum professionals that references the 2014 Ferguson, Missouri, police shooting and subsequent Black Lives Matter protests while describing "objectivity" as a characteristic of "white supremacy culture," which Ginn said was part of its effort to lean towards activism.

SMITHSONIAN PUSHED ‘REVOLTING’ SOCIAL ACTION TRAINING AFTER ‘WHITENESS’ CHART APOLOGY: EXPERT

Reflecting on the testimony, Ginn said it was "very disappointing" and did not represent "a scholarly presentation whatsoever."

"If that's the kind of museum you've been approved to run, then just own it," he said. "Don't say you're being unbiased when it's really evident."

Ginn also criticized Hartig for maintaining that the museum has not taken a side, adding its revised mission statement "changed the purpose of that museum."

During a 2024 presentation to undergraduate and graduate history students, Hartig explained the museum removed the mention of "American history" from its mission statement because it was "hard to get out of the 'America First' mentality."

For Ginn, his visit confirmed what he described as a "massive shift" in the museum profession, with the Smithsonian serving as "the highest-profile symptom of a process that's been going on for some time."

"It is my opinion as a public historian that the mission we've always had is to educate the public and provide scholarly information," he said. "To me, that's what the National Museum of American History should be."

However, Ginn said he is "not hopeful" the institution can change without a "massive effort" to replace current staff with people he believes would prioritize history over politics.

"You're going to have to put in new people who are committed to scholarly standards and non-politicized educational programming," he said. "These people have bought into it, hook, line and sinker."

Fox News Digital reached out to the Smithsonian for comment.

item.title: El-Sayed touts endorsement from pastor who praised notorious antisemite infamous for calling Jews ‘termites’
item.description: Abdul El-Sayed's campaign paid $75,000 in consulting fees to a Detroit pastor who once praised Louis Farrakhan's leadership at a 2013 gathering.
item.content:encoded:
Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is enthusiastically touting the endorsement of Horace Sheffield III, an influential Detroit pastor and radio host who once heaped praise on Nation of Islam minister Louis Farrakhan.

Sheffield endorsed El-Sayed on air in November 2025, with the Senate hopeful issuing a press release to commemorate the occasion and saying that he was "deeply honored" to have his support. In May 2013, Sheffield gave a speech introducing Farrakhan to a gathering of religious leaders where he praised the controversial cleric for his leadership and accused outside forces of slandering him.

"We need someone to give us direction. I believe we have a leader here that can organize us," Sheffield said, referring to Farrakhan, according to a media outlet founded by Farrakhan.

MICHIGAN SENATE RACE: EL-SAYED’S TIES TO EXTREMIST FUEL ANTISEMITISM CONCERNS AMONG JEWISH VOTERS

Before Sheffield lauded the Nation of Islam leader, he had racked up an extensive record of controversial remarks slammed as anti-Semitic or as instances of anti-White racism.

In 1996, for instance, Farrakhan accused Jews of being "wicked deceivers of the American people" who have "sucked their blood." A year later, he suggested that "people will never be free in this country" until they are liberated from the "tremendous amount of influence" Jews exert over the American government.

Shortly before Sheffield praised Farrakhan in May 2013, the Nation of Islam minister stated that "Jews are the most violent of people" in February 2012.

WIFE OF LOUIS FARRAKHAN DEAD AT 90

Farrakhan also called White people "the skunk of the planet earth" and suggested that Europeans are not yet fully evolved human beings.

Following these controversial statements, Sheffield suggested during his 2013 introductory remarks that Farrakhan was a truth teller whom the establishment was trying to silence.

"They want to silence people who tell us the truth, and we know why this is happening and who is doing it, but we need some help with how to overcome it," Sheffield said during his speech.

ABDUL EL-SAYED SAYS RALLYING WITH HASAN PIKER DOESN'T MEAN HE ENDORSES 'AMERICA DESERVED 9/11' REMARK

After the 2013 event, Farrakhan continued his habit of controversial remarks, calling Jews "termites" in 2018.

Despite Sheffield’s praise of a highly controversial cleric, El-Sayed’s campaign has worked with him to a considerable degree.

In June, Sheffield stopped by El-Sayed’s campaign office to film a promotional video for the candidate. More recently, the Washington Free Beacon reported that the El-Sayed campaign had paid a nonprofit run by Sheffield $75,000 for "consulting" fees between October 2025 and June of this year.

Sheffield’s previous radio station suspended him in 2018 after he endorsed Democratic Rep. Shri Thanedar’s failed bid for Michigan governor after accepting tens of thousands of dollars in "consulting" fees from him, according to the Free Beacon.

While Sheffield’s controversial past associations could provide Republicans with ammunition to use against El-Sayed in the general election, especially given the accusations of antisemitism surrounding his campaign, the pastor's endorsement could also help him win the support of Black Michiganders, a demographic he has so far failed to impress.

"I’m deeply honored to have Rev. Sheffield’s support. His lifelong commitment to justice, faith, and service embodies the very best of Detroit," El-Sayed said following the endorsement. "We’re building a coalition that believes politics should be about people, and together we’ll fight to deliver dignity, opportunity, and equity for every Michigander."

Representatives for El-Sayed and Sheffield did not return requests for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Monday.

item.title: GOP party fissures exposed in battle for S.C. Senate seat to replace Graham: 'I don't like hearing that'
item.description: Five GOP candidates clashed over the filibuster, the Iran war, and data centers in South Carolina's heated Senate debate to fill Lindsey Graham's seat.
item.content:encoded:
The five GOP candidates that appeared in South Carolina’s U.S. Senate debate on Monday evening touched on several key issues of national importance as they made their case to fill the seat of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., who died while in office last month.

Although candidates remained united on broad issues of party consensus, the debate exposed a fraying of opinion on topics like the war in Iran, U.S. government spending, the filibuster and datacenter expansion, highlighting the influence of even just one Senate seat.

The candidates include Sen. Darlene Graham Nordone, R-S.C., Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., Rep. Russel Fry, R-S.C., businessman Mark Lynch, and former South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford.

REPUBLICANS DEFY TRUMP, JUMP INTO SOUTH CAROLINA SENATE RACE DESPITE HIS HANDPICKED SUCCESSOR

The biggest clash of the night came from Graham’s own sister, the appointee currently filling his seat.

Nordone, who received President Donald Trump’s endorsement, announced she would vote to end the filibuster — a procedural hurdle that prevents the chamber from passing most legislation without 60 votes. Republicans currently hold 53 seats in the chamber.

"And I am all for — this is where I differ from my brother — getting rid of the filibuster to get this done because eventually the Democrats are going to get rid of it anyway," Nordone said, noting the major break with her late brother.

While supporters of the filibuster argue it prevents parties from strongarming their views into law without bipartisan input, acting as one of the country's last bastions of moderation, the rule has throttled several Republican priorities called for by President Donald Trump, including national voter identification legislation.

Mark Sanford, another candidate who formerly served as governor of South Carolina, also touched on a topic of controversy on Monday by alluding that Congress — not the president’s discretion — should set the direction for the war in Iran.

"Only Congress has the authority to declare war. This decision needs to be made by Congress … body bags don't go back to Washington. They come back to home states and congressional districts," Sanford said.

It has been nearly six months since the U.S originally bombed Iran in coordination with Israel, killing Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. The conflict has stretched well beyond the timeline the administration said it had expected.

WAR POWERS RESOLUTION FAILS AS SENATE REPUBLICANS STAND BY TRUMP ON IRAN

In the time since, debate among lawmakers has raged over whether the president has overstepped his authority and started a war — a power granted to Congress under the U.S. Constitution — and whether lawmakers should pass legislation to restrict his abilities.

Besides Sanford, other candidates seemed to support Trump, citing a concern over Iran’s nuclear capabilities.

One candidate, Rep. Russell Fry, R-S.C., qualified that support by affirming he would not support deploying U.S. servicemembers to the area.

"No boots on the ground. I’m not a believer in that. My brother served in Iraq, and I’ve lost friends in foreign wars. But we can finish the mission by defanging Iran and making sure they have no capabilities left," Fry said.

On yet another area of division, Mark Lynch, a South Carolina businessman, raised the issue of datacenters, a somewhat niche policy concern that’s rapidly raising questions of how national security interests are balanced against local interests and energy consumption.

While Republicans remain split on the issue, Lynch said he would favor prioritizing local community concerns.

"It is a pain point for South Carolinians," Lynch said, referring to the expansion of the centers.

"We're tired of waking up and seeing 100 acres of trees bulldozed, and we're told the data center is going to go right next to our neighborhood. It is horrible noise pollution. They're robbing our water. It takes millions of gallons to cool the data centers, and it's causing our electric utilities to increase. We already have a problem with inflation and affordability."

Although the debate remained largely restrained, Nordone needled Lynch in her closing remarks over several criticisms of her brother.

Lynch had criticized the late senator’s track record on amnesty and the legalization of marijuana.

"Mr. Lynch mentioned Lindsey Graham multiple times, and I don't know if he's just afraid Lindsey beat him and now his little sister is going to beat him. But I just don't like hearing that," Nordone said.

Lynch ran against Linsey Graham in the 2026 primary earlier this year, before his death. Graham soundly defeated Lynch in a 56.8% to 28.9% win in June.

WATCH: DEMOCRATS ADMIT WHEN THEY'D ELIMINATE THE FILIBUSTER AS SAVE ACT FIGHT HEATS UP

Lynch did not have an opportunity to respond.

With the debate now concluded, the Republican who wins the primary later this month will go on to run in the state’s Nov. 3 general election against Democratic nominee Annie Andrews — a race that’s projected to heavily favor the GOP. The primary, set for Aug. 11, will likely decide which Republican will go on to win a full six-year term in November.

item.title: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle's royal 'rupture' caused 'very serious damage' to the monarchy: author
item.description: Royal commentators debate whether Meghan Markle could have succeeded in the royal family as the duchess celebrates her 45th birthday amid an unhealed rift.
item.content:encoded:
As Meghan Markle celebrates her 45th birthday, one royal author argues the Duchess of Sussex's exit from royal life caused "very serious damage" to the monarchy.

"I believe that the rupture in the family that saw Meghan and Harry go to the United States has done very serious damage to the monarchy," Catherine Mayer, who penned "Divide & Rule," told Fox News Digital.

"But to say that is not to say that I blame them for what happened," she said. "It's often taken as a criticism: 'Look what they've done to the monarchy.' I think this has been very painful for everybody and for the institution, but you need only look at the latest polling on the popularity of the monarchy to see that it is losing ground."

PRINCE HARRY LONGS FOR HIS OLD ROYAL LIFE AS AMERICA ISN'T WHAT HE EXPECTED, EXPERTS SAY

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex stepped back as senior royals in 2020, citing intrusive British media coverage and a lack of support from the palace. After moving to California, they aired their grievances in interviews and documentaries. Harry's 2023 memoir, "Spare," further strained his relationship with the family.

In July, the former American actress had planned to accompany her husband during several engagements on his return to the U.K. However, security concerns prevented Meghan and their two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, from making the full trip.

While the Sussexes had a private meeting with King Charles and Queen Camilla on July 10, marking the first time since 2022 that Meghan had returned to England, she didn't make any public appearances.

WATCH: PRINCE HARRY AND MEGHAN MARKLE'S EXIT HURT THE MONARCHY: AUTHOR

The couple lost their taxpayer-funded security when they stepped down as working royals. The Duke of Sussex has long sought to have it reinstated, citing concerns for his family's safety.

Mayer argued that, according to U.K. polls, the royal family has lost popularity primarily due to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, who was stripped of his princely title following his controversial relationship with late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. However, she believes that "undoubtedly," the Sussexes had an ability to connect with younger populations in a way that’s "not really there with the rest of the family."

"The only ones who can potentially do it are Kate and William, and they're more of a small 'c' conservative in their approach," said Mayer, referring to the Prince and Princess of Wales.

"They're young, but they're in their 40s," she said. "Their children are really young. And there's nobody in between George and his parents, William and Kate, to capture the imagination of younger audiences. Harry and Meghan are basically the same age, but they had this appeal, a much broader appeal, and that's been lost now."

Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner echoed that view, noting that family divisions remain unresolved despite recent signs of reconciliation.

"I feel there are major cracks in the royal family over Meghan and Harry, especially between King Charles and Prince William, who I believe are at loggerheads over the couple, culminating in the recent private meeting at Highgrove, leaving William blindsided about the meeting. Now, with Harry able to use Buckingham Palace again when he returns, it could be a breakthrough for Meghan and a heart-piercing wound for William."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

While Meghan's relationship with King Charles reportedly softened following their private family reunion this summer, multiple reports continue to describe her ties with William and Kate as distant, with little evidence the broader royal rift has fully healed.

"In my book, I also examine the bullying allegations made against Meghan," said Mayer. "One of the problems was that they surfaced at exactly the time of the 2021 Oprah Winfrey interview. I think that made a lot of people suspect this was done to undercut anything Meghan might say in the interview. I'd actually been hearing about friction in the palace for a very long time before the story surfaced. As I explain in the book, that doesn't necessarily mean we're talking about bullying, but we're definitely talking about real friction there."

"We're talking about people who were very bruised by the experience, which includes her as well," Mayer continued. "But the fact is, there were real frictions between the brothers, William and Harry, as well as between the women and within the palace system. I don't think Meghan really understood that the monarchy will always give preference to the monarch and the immediate heir. And its members get very nervous when somebody feels bigger and more glamorous than the institution."

"The last thing they wanted to do was make her into some big star," Mayer added.

Turner noted that Meghan hasn't been the only one to experience struggles with "The Firm."

"Outsiders are accepted, provided they do not become more powerful or overshadow family members," he said. "In my time, Charles used to hate being overshadowed by Princess Diana at walkabouts. I believe this was part of the reason for the breakup. I feel palace employees and members of the royal family could see Meghan's charm was making her into another Diana in waiting."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Still, British royal expert Hilary Fordwich said mistakes made by the Sussexes cannot be overlooked and have contributed to their estrangement from the royal family.

"Harry and Meghan didn't just make a silly mistake," Fordwich told Fox News Digital. "They have undertaken a fundamentally damaging, deliberate strategy to undermine the royals, which is unforgivable. The Firm was most welcoming to her, bent the rules for her, made exceptions for her, but she thwarted it all. She didn't want to either learn or accept advice. King Charles and Prince William now have a narrower, more disciplined monarchy as a result."

"Yes, things could have been very different if Meghan had been dedicated to duty and not to herself and her own aggrandizement," said Fordwich.

British broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard also told Fox News Digital that the secret to being a successful member of the British royal family is to adapt quickly.

"The House of Windsor may appear rigid, but it has run like clockwork and survived through history," said Chard. "The one thing people marrying into The Firm have to learn is to adapt. Both Princess Catherine and Meghan came in as outsiders. But one chose to learn the institution. The system is tough, but the system also gave Meghan support. The system can't save someone who won't play ball. The institution expects sacrifice before platform."

"Harry himself also talked about leaving royal life for years. Meghan gave him that push. Better handling could have delayed it, but I don't think it would have prevented it."

Mayer pointed out that Meghan was facing an uphill battle from the very beginning.

"When I was writing this book, I really did go back and challenge my own assumptions about whether Meghan could have ever made a go of it," said Mayer. "And I concluded that it was highly unlikely, and not her fault — or certainly not entirely her fault. One of the things people always say to me is, 'Of course she Googled Harry before they started dating. Of course, she knew about it.'"

"I've been covering the monarchy for a very long time. I'm also the biographer of Charles, the man who is now King. I've spent a lot of time behind the scenes. Even after all the time I've spent there, I'm still surprised by the strangeness of the culture and how unlike any other culture it is."

Mayer also recalled when Meghan received criticism for mimicking how she curtsied to the late Queen Elizabeth II in the Netflix docuseries "Harry & Meghan." However, audiences missed the point, she said.

"How weird it is to have a family where, even in private, you not only curtsy to the monarch, but you also follow an order of precedence," said Mayer. "How would anybody be prepared for that? The monarchy is essentially a medieval institution with some modern features grafted onto it."

Chard said "the damage has been done" following Meghan and Harry's departure. She noted the royal family has "moved on," prioritizing the future. While there will always be hope for reconciliation, she said, it will take time on all sides.

"Trust takes years to rebuild," she said.

item.title: Why Trump is downplaying reports Russia and China are helping Iran
item.description: Trump says he'll ask Putin directly about satellite imagery allegations as experts warn Russia and China are quietly aiding Iran against U.S. forces.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump cast doubt in recent days on allegations that Russia is helping Iran target U.S. forces, even as members of his own administration acknowledge Moscow and Beijing are supporting Tehran in other ways.

Trump dismissed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's claim that Russia supplied Iran with satellite imagery of U.S. military installations in the Gulf, saying any assistance would have been "very unimpactful" given the damage inflicted on Iran's military.

"We’ll find out if that’s true. I’ll ask Putin. We’ll find out," Trump told reporters at the end of July.

WALTZ WARNS OF CHINESE, RUSSIAN-FUELED ‘NATIONAL SECURITY THREAT’ LOOMING CLOSE TO US SHORES

"I don’t think they’ve been doing it, certainly not at a high level," Trump added. "And if they have, it has been very unimpactful."

Trump pointed to the damage Iran’s military has suffered during the war. Russian help, he argued, has failed to stop the United States from destroying much of Tehran’s conventional forces.

Trump's comments came as his administration confront separate reports that Russia and China are helping Iran in different ways — allegations that, if borne out, would suggest America's two chief geopolitical rivals are quietly supporting a nation at war with the U.S. Members of his own administration have acknowledged broader help from Moscow and Beijing.

CHINA’S IRAN TIES COMPLICATE TRUMP-XI SUMMIT AS TENSIONS TEST US LEVERAGE

War Secretary Pete Hegseth has said Russia and China are "enabling some of the things Iran is doing," but a White House official told Fox News Digital that any foreign assistance has failed to improve Tehran's ability to attack Americans.

Trump's comments came in response to two recent reports: Zelenskyy's allegation that Russia provided satellite intelligence to Iran and a Reuters report that China could send hundreds of shoulder-fired air-defense missiles to Tehran through Pakistan, which China has denied.

Fresh satellite imagery could help Iran locate high-value assets and refine strike coordinates, then show whether an attack hit its intended target.

"As the President stated, nothing that any outside actor is doing to help Iran is in any way increasing their ability to target Americans," the official told Fox News Digital, responding to questions about Zelenskyy's claim that Russia gave Iran satellite imagery of U.S. military installations in the Gulf.

Zelenskyy laid out Ukraine's evidence Saturday, saying Russian satellites had surveyed Gulf countries and U.S. military installations beginning in early July before the imagery later appeared in Iran.

"These images subsequently appear in Iran," Zelenskyy wrote on X.

Ukraine found what Zelenskyy described as a "clear correlation" between the Russian observations and subsequent Iranian attacks. According to Zelenskyy, Moscow collected imagery before strikes to aid targeting and returned afterward to assess the damage.

Zelenskyy said Russian satellites focused on four air bases over two days — two in Bahrain and one each in Jordan and Kuwait — and said Ukrainian intelligence had shared the information with foreign partners.

Ukraine’s ambassador to the U.S., Olga Stefanishyna, said at a July 30 reporter roundtable that the allegation did not arise during Zelenskyy’s White House meeting with Trump because the agenda was crowded. She said Ukraine had provided the information "through other channels."

A Ukrainian official told Fox News Digital that Kyiv wants to avoid "opening a second front" with Iran.

Hegseth acknowledged Russian and Chinese support for Iran during a Senate hearing in July.

There was "definitely adversary alignment," Hegseth said. Russia and China were "at different levels, enabling some of the things Iran is doing."

The U.S. has ways to deter that support, he added, though some of those measures should remain classified. Hegseth said earlier in the war that the administration knew "exactly" what Moscow and Beijing were doing and was addressing their actions where needed.

Russia has denied supplying Iran with intelligence on American military targets. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said the locations of U.S. bases were publicly available. The Kremlin also dismissed earlier reporting about Russian intelligence support for Iran as false.

Trump also questioned reports that Iran could soon receive hundreds of Chinese-made shoulder-fired air-defense systems through Pakistan, saying Chinese President Xi Jinping had assured him Beijing would stay out of the conflict.

"That was surprising. I mean, things like that happen, but that would be surprising. He told me very strongly he wouldn’t partake, but he knows I’d be quite disappointed. He’s coming here, I think, on September 24," the president told reporters Wednesday.

Matthew Kroenig, a former Pentagon and intelligence official, called the reports "highly plausible," pointing to growing cooperation among Russia, China and Iran.

"From Russia and China’s point of view, if they can complicate the U.S. war in the Middle East and raise the cost to Washington, that’s a good thing for them," Kroenig told Fox News Digital.

Kroenig said Trump may be warning Moscow and Beijing privately instead of confronting them before television cameras.

"That might be the most generous interpretation, that it’s his way of warning China and Russia to knock it off," he said.

Trump’s comments would carry more risk if the president were relying on assurances from Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, Kroenig said. He urged the administration to make clear that either country would face a cost for helping Tehran.

"I think there would be a risk to just discounting this altogether," Kroenig said.

Anna Borshchevskaya, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, said Moscow has spent years building closer military ties with Tehran.

"If this proves accurate, Russia has found a way to help Iran without direct military engagement, and that’s why this is significant," Borshchevskaya told Fox News Digital.

Iran began supplying Russia with Shahed attack drones in 2022, giving Moscow a cheap weapon it could launch in waves against Ukrainian cities and power infrastructure.

Russia later began producing its own versions with Iranian support and improved the design, making the drones a mainstay of its attacks. Tehran’s earlier support now hangs over Zelenskyy’s claim that Moscow is helping Iran target American forces.

Satellite imagery would give Moscow another way to aid Tehran while avoiding a direct clash with American forces.

"It’s hard to think how the provision of intelligence is insignificant," Borshchevskaya said.

She said Trump may be trying to keep his public exchanges with Moscow calm as U.S. officials send firmer messages in private.

Russia views the wars in Ukraine and Iran as connected parts of its campaign against American influence, Borshchevskaya said. U.S. officials tend to handle each conflict through a separate policy process.

"The challenge for us is that we often separate theaters, but Russia does not," she said. "Russia looks at all of these conflicts in a much more interconnected way."

Borshchevskaya said Russia has chosen forms of aid that can strengthen Iran without committing Russian troops or entering a direct fight with Washington.

"Russia is being restrained here," she said. "They’re playing a much more nuanced game."

Trump also voiced surprise Wednesday at a report that Iran could soon receive hundreds of Chinese-made, shoulder-fired air-defense systems through Pakistan.

"That was surprising. I mean, things like that happen, but that would be surprising," Trump said.

Xi had given Trump a firm assurance that China would stay out of the war, according to the president.

"He told me very strongly he wouldn’t partake, but he knows I’d be quite disappointed," Trump said.

China called the report "groundless." Pakistan rejected the claim that it would help route the weapons to Iran, calling the allegation "baseless and devoid of truth."

Kroenig said Beijing has supplied Russia with economic and industrial support during the war in Ukraine. China has stopped short of openly sending lethal weapons, a limit he had expected Beijing to observe in the Iran war.

Advanced air defenses would require approval from the Chinese government, he said. Russian satellite intelligence would also come from state-controlled capabilities.

"There are no mom-and-pop shops in St. Petersburg selling this data," Kroenig said.

item.title: MORNING GLORY: President Trump’s triple bogey
item.description: Trump ordered a major escalation of combat with Iran last weekend only to call it off via Truth Social, marking his second reversal on IRGC operations.
item.content:encoded:
Pardon the extended analogy ahead, but as President Donald Trump is easily the best golfer among all presidents, it plays well.

Don’t believe me about the best golfer assessment? Ask ChatGPT or any AI agent. It isn’t even remotely a close question.

Having been a caddy since 1966, I’ve carried lots of clubs, raked plenty of traps and held many pins. "Pipeline Joe Day" was the best senior I’ve ever caddied for, and he earned his nickname among the golf gophers because he drove 16 or 17 out of 18 fairways or greens well into his 80s, but as he lost distance when he crossed over the octogenarian mark, the birdies mostly went away. Even the best short games among seniors can save par but won’t make many birdies.

TRUMP IS WINNING EVERY BATTLE IN IRAN—AND RISKING THE WAR THAT MATTERS

President Trump can routinely shave a stroke off of par on any given hole, and it wouldn’t surprise if there is an eagle or two every month of rounds.

But, as no golfer is perfect, the president is bound to have had some awful rounds and some very bad holes. Not "Tin Cup" Kevin Costner bad, but bad. He must go "OB" on his drive at least occasionally, and a three putt on top of hitting three off the tee…well, that’s usually triple bogey land for even very good amateurs and most pros.

Like even the greatest golfers, every president yanks a decision or three almost every round. If a president has ever had a perfect month of perfect days, I’m unaware of it. So mistakes will be made, and President Trump made a big one this past weekend.

TRUMP WARNS IRAN FIGHTING ISN'T OVER AS HE VOWS US WILL 'WIN' AS TALKS FADE

"Reliable reports from a variety of sources confirm that President Trump had ordered a major escalation of combat with Iran for this past weekend only to call it off late Saturday night. Some of our allies were primed to participate, but others urged a delay."

It is the second time President Trump has called off a return to major combat operations that would continue uninterrupted for the weeks it would take to try and break the rump regime in Iran run by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps ("IRGC.") Pay almost no attention to the civilian puppets of the rump regime. It is a military dictatorship inside Iran now.

"We just want to win," President Trump declared at the Cabinet meeting in Camp David last week. That was a clear and candid declaration of the end game: A return to the genuinely open Strait of Hormuz coupled with a verifiable abandonment of the Iranian regime’s decades-long drive for nuclear weapons.

MORNING GLORY: PRESIDENT TRUMP, IRAN AND NAPOLEON’S STILL-RELEVANT MAXIM

President Trump knows that the IRGC lies and that the IRGC cheats. He has said many times that the regime’s negotiators will spend hours talking about the nuclear program in closed meetings, and then immediately walk to the microphones and declare the nuclear program was not discussed at all in the same meetings.

"They are scum," he has said. Secretary of State Rubio has declared, "These people are crazy." Both are correct.

The original MOU was worth a try. I always thought it signaled halftime in the battle and that after the midterm elections in the U.S., President Trump would demand the immediate implementation of a rigorous inspections regime at every site known or suspected of harboring part of Iran’s nuclear weapons program — including "Pickaxe Mountain" — as the necessary conditions without which major combat operations would resume and continue indefinitely to batter the shaky regime until it crumbled in real time.

But the IRGC came out of the locker room first and broke the MOU. Since then, they have again broken an agreement to trade a ceasefire for an open Strait and layered on a surprise attack on our military in Jordan. They are the polar opposite of "good faith" bargainers and always have been.

There is no reason to believe that the IRGC will not lie and cheat again. It is who they are and who they have always been since Ayatollah Khomeini led the revolution to topple the Shah in 1979. Since then, the Iranian regime’s negotiators have fooled both President Carter and President Obama in a comprehensive fashion and other presidents to some degree, but they have never fooled Donald Trump.

Until this past weekend. The president launched a huge slice past the out-of-bounds markers. Everyone saw it. Everyone knows the president is hitting three on the tee now.

Can he scramble and save par? Yes, because it’s a long par 5. Can he win the match in a decisive way? Yes, but not if he keeps playing this way. Not if he gets the yips again.

Everyone who has ever caddied for a very good golfer in match play should know the truth of the scorecard mid-round, as well as the potential to turn that match around, sometimes quickly. But only the president can do that. Not our allies. Not his advisors. Certainly not the legacy media.

Donald Trump has been surprising and indeed startling his critics for his nearly dozen years in politics. Hope he has at least one more huge surprise in store.

item.title: LIZ PEEK: Michigan can stop the socialist fever rage — or watch it swallow the Senate
item.description: Abdul El-Sayed and Haley Stevens face off in Michigan's most expensive Democratic Senate primary ever, with control of the U.S. Senate at stake.
item.content:encoded:
On Tuesday, Michigan voters have a final shot at shutting down the socialist surge that is convulsing the Democratic Party and alarming the country. Polls and prediction markets suggest they will not do so.

Tuesday is the final day for voters in the Democratic primary to choose a U.S. Senate candidate for November. The primary winner will face former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers for the seat currently held by Sen. Gary Peters, who is retiring. Although Mallory McMorrow remains on the ballot after suspending her campaign, the contest has effectively narrowed to establishment-backed Rep. Haley Stevens and progressive Abdul El-Sayed. Stevens has represented Michigan’s 11th Congressional District since 2019.

It is, to paraphrase Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, a choice between normal and crazy. El-Sayed, who wants to abolish ICE, eliminate oil and gas, ban school choice, deny arms shipments to U.S. ally Israel, sharply raise taxes, provide tuition-free four-year college degrees and establish a wealth tax, will likely win the primary. Stevens, in contrast, is a normal liberal Democrat.

DEM PRIMARY ERUPTS AS ESTABLISHMENT FAVORITE DISMISSES RIVAL AS ‘CELEBRITY CANDIDATE’

Why should you care? Because the critical Michigan contest could well determine whether Democrats take over the Senate in November and effectively shut down the Trump agenda. 

If you agree that there is much more work to do to strengthen our immigration laws, make American energy permanently accessible, level the trade playing field for U.S. companies, purge our welfare programs of fraud, appoint more conservative judges, promote new industries and improve our health care system, you will not want to see the virtual end of the Trump presidency.

That is what is at stake.

The Michigan race will also indicate whether the progressive left — the ideological home of the Democratic Socialists of America — has the support of mainstream voters in a Midwestern purple state or instead represents a fringe element born of an intellectually bankrupt Democratic Party whose sole message for the past 12 years has been its hatred of President Trump.

SOCIALISM’S RISE INSIDE THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY NOW THREATENS THE AMERICAN DREAM

If El-Sayed wins the primary but is defeated in the November election, the progressive left will lose steam and have less say in choosing the Democratic presidential nominee in 2028.

That would be good for Democrats and good for the United States.

It would also be good for Israel and for American Jews. The Michigan contest is as much about support for the Middle East’s only democracy and a close U.S. ally as it is about tax policy or Medicare for All, which El-Sayed endorses. AIPAC, the pro-Israel lobbying group, and affiliated groups have spent about $30 million supporting Stevens and opposing El-Sayed in the race, which has already become the most expensive Democratic Senate primary in history.

JEWISH MICHIGAN DEMOCRATS ADMIT THEY WILL VOTE REPUBLICAN IF ABDUL EL-SAYED BECOMES NOMINEE

The race is a proxy battle for the heart of the Democratic Party, pitting El-Sayed supporters Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Reps. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., against popular Michigan Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Peters, all of whom are backing Stevens.

Stevens’ supporters claim she has a better chance of beating Rogers in the fall than El-Sayed does. RealClearPolling averages support that claim, showing Stevens leading Rogers in a potential November matchup while El-Sayed narrowly trails him.

Republican Rogers ran for the Senate before, losing by only half a percentage point to Democrat Elissa Slotkin, a former CIA analyst and Defense Department employee. At the time, Democrats had lost only two Senate seats in 52 years. Many of these Senate races were fiercely competitive, which was not surprising. Michigan is an authentic swing state. Trump won the state in 2016, lost it to Joe Biden in 2020 and won it again in 2024.

Rogers, a veteran, a seven-term congressman and a businessman, is campaigning with the endorsement of President Donald Trump, as he did in 2024.

Michigan holds open primaries, prompting speculation that Republicans might cross party lines to vote for El-Sayed, thinking the inexperienced Muslim candidate would be easier to beat in November. There is no evidence that this is happening.

Another quirk of the race is that the UAW has endorsed El-Sayed, despite his opponent’s ties to the auto industry. Stevens served as chief of staff for the Presidential Task Force on the Auto Industry, "the federal initiative that helped save General Motors, Chrysler, and over 200,000 Michigan jobs during the Great Recession." In addition, she helped build the Office of Recovery for Automotive Communities and Workers in the Obama White House.

In contrast, El-Sayed has no real ties to the auto industry or its workers. Since expanding to include more than 100,000 higher education workers, the UAW has been hijacked by leftist elements. The union recently endorsed a candidate in a New York City Democratic primary who ran on a platform opposing federal highway spending and embracing public transportation. The UAW endorsement does not mean what it used to.

El-Sayed has not declared himself a member of the DSA but shares many attributes with that group’s newly elected candidates. Some of his funding, like that of former Maine Senate candidate Graham Platner, has come from his family, with his father-in-law, a nephrologist at a Detroit hospital, donating $300,000 to an independent super PAC supporting his candidacy. He is also campaigning with Hasan Piker, the far-left antisemite who once said that America deserved the 9/11 terrorist attacks, which killed thousands.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

And, like other progressives, El-Sayed’s résumé is paper-thin. He was appointed executive director and health officer of the Detroit Health Department in 2015 but resigned in 2017 to run for governor of Michigan. He came in second in the 2018 primary. He worked for the Wayne County Department of Health, Human, and Veterans Services starting in 2023 but left two years later to run for the Senate. He points to his emergency leadership of the county’s scandal-plagued juvenile detention facility as a key accomplishment, but local news fact-checkers have scrutinized that claim as overstating the extent of the recovery.

The star-struck liberal media have unsurprisingly spent little time investigating his performance in those two posts.

If he wins, that will change, and El-Sayed’s spotty and opportunistic record will become campaign fodder. He is favored by young, white, anti-Israel liberals. Whether that group can propel him across the finish line in November is questionable.

We fervently hope not.

item.title: Socialist insurgents eye Midwest gains as Dem civil war threatens must-hold Senate seat
item.description: Abdul El-Sayed and Haley Stevens clash in the most expensive Democratic Senate primary in history, with over $80 million spent and AIPAC at the center.
item.content:encoded:
DETROIT, MI - The high-stakes fight between the left-wing and the center-left establishment for the future of the Democratic Party is front-and-center on Tuesday in Michigan's primary.

Boosted by a string of victories this spring in mostly blue congressional districts across the country, the Democrats' ideological war moves to the Great Lakes battleground state, where progressive victories could reshape the party and endanger must-hold seats in the midterm elections.

Also at stake as Michigan joins Kansas, Missouri, Virginia and Washington State in holding mid-summer primaries is President Donald Trump's immense clout over the GOP and the power of his endorsements in Republican nominating contests.

But taking top billing is Michigan's divisive and expensive Democratic Senate primary, which is seen as the biggest stage to date in the fierce fight for the future of the Democratic Party.

THE MIDTERM SENATE RACES THAT COULD FLIP THE BALANCE OF POWER IN CONGRESS

"This is ground zero in the battle for the future of the Democratic Party pitting status quo corporate Democrats against shake up the system economic fighters, and we’ll see who wins," Adam Green, co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee (PCCC), a leading group on the left, told Fox News Digital.

The primary face-off pits Abdul El-Sayed, a former Wayne County Health Department director, against Rep. Haley Stevens, a more moderate candidate backed by the establishment. The race to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters, who is backing Stevens, is a must-hold for the Democrats and one of roughly a dozen Senate races from coast to coast that will determine if Republicans hold onto their slim Senate majority.

Matt Bennett, one of the leaders at the Third Way, a leading center-left Democratic organization, told Fox News Digital the Michigan showdown is "the first time the left is competing for a swing seat" and warned, "the significance is it could really put this seat in jeopardy."

El-Sayed, who, if elected, would make history as the nation's first Muslim senator, is an epidemiologist who unsuccessfully ran for governor as an insurgent candidate in 2018. He has made support for "Medicare-for-all" a major component of his campaign.

The far-left candidate has also called for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and is a vocal critic of Israel amid its war with Hamas — even characterizing Israel's actions in Gaza as "genocide" against Palestinians.

MIKE ROGERS ARGUES ABDUL EL-SAYED IS 'A SPECIAL SAUCE OF CRAZY'

And El-Sayed, who is backed by top far-left leaders and teamed with progressive champions Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York on the Michigan campaign trail two weeks ago, and who served as a top surrogate on Sanders' 2020 presidential campaign, has vowed not to accept PAC donations.

Stevens, who flipped a GOP-held district in her 2018 election to Congress, is backed by top national and Michigan Democrats, including Peters, term-limited Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, and longtime Senate Democratic Leader Sen. Chuck Schumer.

Schumer and the party establishment view Stevens as more electable than El-Sayed, who has sparked controversy with his past comments.

"I am the best Democrat to go forward. I am the only person in this race who has won tough primaries multiple times. You know, running with the Michigan grit, resilience and determination," Stevens told Fox News Digital on Sunday, as she teamed up with Peters on the campaign trail.

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

Over $80 million has been spent on the primary showdown, making it the most expensive Democratic Senate nomination race in history. Much of the money has been shelled out by outside groups in support of Stevens and against El-Sayed. The biggest spending comes from United Democracy Project, a political action committee aligned with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC).

El-Sayed, who has repeatedly attacked Stevens over the massive infusion of AIPAC-linked money, told reporters on Sunday, "If you need $70 million to come in here and help get you elected, then the question has to be, are you actually electable on your own terms."

The winner will face off in the midterms against former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers, who is on a glidepath to win the GOP Senate nomination.

The Trump-backed Rogers, who lost the 2024 Senate election in Michigan by a razor-thin margin, said in a Fox News Digital interview that he doesn't care whom he faces-off with in November.

"It doesn't matter to us. We've looked at both candidates. We feel confident we're going to beat either one of those candidates that come out of that race," Rogers highlighted.

And Rogers claimed, "They are very radical, and they are way too extreme for Michigan. I mean, Abdul, he has his own special sauce of crazy."

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

But Democrats are confident they can regroup after a combustible primary.

"Let's make sure that anyone but Mike Rogers gets to the United States Senate," Stevens told reporters on Sunday. "After the primary, you're going to see a united Democratic Party. You are going to see us going full force, full fledged ahead."

And El-Sayed told Fox News Digital, "I think we all understand the risk of Donald Trump. We all understand the risk of Mike Rogers."

The left-wing versus establishment battle is also playing out in Michigan's 7th Congressional District, a key Republican-controlled swing seat race that's among roughly two-dozen that will impact whether the GOP holds onto its fragile House majority.

William Lawrence, a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, which advocates for political action to tackle climate change, is on the rise against two more moderate Democrats. Lawrence is backed by Sanders and El-Sayed, as well as some top progressive groups. The primary winner will face GOP Rep. Tom Barrett in the general election.

The party civil war is also on display in Michigan's deep blue 13th Congressional District.

MEET THE FAR LEFT INSURGENTS WAGING WAR ON THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY IN THE 2026 MIDTERMS

Rep. Shri Thanedar, who is supported by top House Democratic leaders, is being challenged by state Rep. Donovan McKinney, who is backed by Sanders, El-Sayed, and Squad members Reps. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts, and Summer Lee of Pennsylvania.

And the ideological warfare is also front-and-center in Missouri, in the state's St. Louis-based and heavily Democratic 1st Congressional District.

Rep. Wesley Bell is facing off in a rematch against former Rep. Cori Bush, a Squad member who Bell ousted in the 2024 primary.

Trump's endorsements are getting tested in two statewide showdowns on Tuesday, in Michigan and Kansas.

The president is backing Rep. John James in Michigan's GOP gubernatorial primary. James, a West Point graduate and one-time Republican rising star, is facing off against multi-millionaire businessman Perry Johnson, a former gubernatorial and presidential candidate.

The winner will take on likely Democratic nominee and current Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, in the race to succeed Whitmer.

In Kansas, Trump is supporting state Senate President Ty Masterson in a crowded field of Republican gubernatorial contenders.

Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly is term-limited, which makes the race to succeed her a top flip opportunity for the GOP.

In Washington State, the marquee primary showdown is in the state's 3rd Congressional District, where Democratic Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, a former auto shop co-owner, is facing a crowded field of challengers from both parties.

Washington state has a top-two primary system in which all candidates, regardless of party, compete on the same ballot and the two highest vote-getters move on to the general election.

The race is another crucial House showdown that may decide the chamber's majority.

In Virginia, voters head to the polls to cast ballots in Senate primaries and in a handful of House primaries in extremely competitive districts that may impact the balance of power on Capitol Hill.

item.title: I was a female athlete, now I fight for them in court. We need more Sophie Cunninghams
item.description: Sophie Cunningham's ESPN interview defending girls against biological male athletes has sparked a nationwide debate over Title IX and fair play.
item.content:encoded:
Sports have played a crucial role throughout my life. Growing up, I ran cross-country and was coached by my dad in basketball, until I found my true love: volleyball. I loved being a setter to the point that I dreamed about making plays. It taught me the things a sport often does: willpower, loyalty, discipline and how to come back swinging when you get knocked down.

But what I remember most is simply how much I loved it. My obsession even dictated the college I chose, where a devastating injury broke my heart and ended my career. There’s one thing I feel obligated to tell you, though: I was never going to be a collegiate star.

I went to a small school, and I still stand today at my maximum height of 5 feet flat. What I lacked in stature, I assure you, I did not lack in heart. I was a scrappy competitor, and I took losses hard. (Some would say I still do.) I embraced every morning and late night, the bruises and broken bones — not because I was destined to be Division I, but simply because I loved it.

JEMELE HILL TAKES AIM AT SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM AS STORM CONTROVERSY GROWS OVER GIRLS SUPPORTING WOMEN’S SPORTS

I gained friendships, grit, and drive I’m confident I wouldn’t have gained elsewhere. And I say this, admittedly, not as a promising up-and-comer, but just a girl who loved playing. I step into a different court these days, but I still carry the grit that women’s athletics gave me when I walk into a courtroom.

Enter Sophie Cunningham.

In a now-famous ESPN interview, the Indiana Fever star, who calls herself politically "very much in the middle," said she wants to protect young girls "who shouldn’t have to go against biological men." With that love, she added, comes truth.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM DOUBLES DOWN AHEAD OF SUN GAME AFTER ESPN PROFILE STIRS CONTROVERSY: 'I SAID WHAT I SAID'

After the media clutched their pearls over her saying biological sex is real, she doubled down, called it "common sense," and posted on Instagram saying, "I said what I said." No apology tour. No caveats. Just the truth, said twice for the people in the back. Her bold stand has sparked an important nationwide conversation in the days since and a whole gamut of supporters and detractors.

This is the courage aspiring female athletes need, especially in a league that partners with Girls in the Game, which says that one of its values is "moving beyond the binary of ‘girl.’" Tell that to the girl who sacrificed everything to reach the podium.

Women’s sports had a banner year. In two cases Alliance Defending Freedom litigated alongside the courageous leadership of Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador and West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey, the U.S. Supreme Court unanimously held that sex matters and that states can protect women’s sports under Title IX. That’s a win for every girl in those 27 states.

'SAVE WOMEN'S SPORTS' LEGAL DEFENSE AND TRANS ATHLETE'S ATTORNEYS SPEAK OUT AFTER LANDMARK SCOTUS RULING

But what does this mean for Kallie Keeler in Washington, who had to report a sexual assault after competing against a male wrestler during a match? For Selina Soule, Chelsea Mitchell, Alanna Smith, and Ashley Nicoletti, still waiting for Connecticut to stand up for the girls who are losing to boys today? For girls in California forced to compete against biologically male athletes like AB Hernandez?

It means we’re coming for the 23 remaining states. A girl’s equal opportunity shouldn’t hinge on her ZIP code. Our daughters deserve better than lawyers who can’t define what a woman is — better than professional athletes with platforms who think it’s fine for men to steal the podium from the girls coming up behind them.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

And they deserve far better than a WNBA co-owner swearing at them for holding a sign that read, "Thank you, Sophie, for speaking up for girls!" The newly suspended Seattle Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton forgot that love tells the truth.

But Sophie remembered. At the height of her career, she took a stand for truth while others chose cowardice. Speaking truth should be praised, not punished.

There are young girls who dream of being the next big star. And there are also girls who just love the game like I did. They all deserve fair play. Where are the women willing to stand up, inspire greatness, and tell the truth? Ladies, we’re pointing the finger at you.

item.title: Washington man arrested on arson charge tied to devastating Spokane wildfire
item.description: A man was arrested and charged with arson on Monday in connection with the Old Trails Fire in the Spokane area in Washington state, police said.
item.content:encoded:
A Washington state man was arrested Monday on a first-degree arson charge in connection with the Old Trails Fire, one of several wildfires that have destroyed hundreds of structures and forced tens of thousands of people to evacuate the Spokane area, authorities said.

Aaron F. Farinacci, 37, was taken into custody after Spokane County Sheriff’s Office detectives and Washington Department of Natural Resources investigators developed probable cause to arrest him, according to the sheriff’s office.

Citizen tips and information from Airway Heights police officers and Spokane County sheriff’s deputies who responded to the initial call and conducted evacuations helped lead investigators to Farinacci, the sheriff’s office said.

Authorities described Farinacci as a convicted felon from Arizona but said they had found no documented criminal history involving fires.

Investigators have not connected Farinacci to the two other major blazes burning in the area, the Autumn Lane and Fairview fires, officials said.

PALISADES FIRE SUSPECT ALLEGEDLY DRIVEN BY 'SOCIETAL REVENGE,' BEHAVIORAL ANALYST TESTIFIES IN COURT

"We will be looking into any other crimes Mr. Farinacci may have committed in the past," Spokane County Sheriff John Nowels said during a news briefing.

Nowels said first-degree arson was the charge supported by probable cause at that stage of the investigation and cautioned that the case could change as authorities gathered additional evidence.

Detectives obtained an arrest warrant for Farinacci and a search warrant for his residence in the 2800 block of West Elliott Drive, according to the sheriff’s office.

Deputies served the warrant Monday and arrested Farinacci without incident. Authorities said detectives found a butane lighter and waterproof matches while detaining and searching him.

SPENCER PRATT REACTS TO SPOKANE DEVASTATION WITH BLUNT WILDFIRE WARNING AND MESSAGE OF FAITH

Farinacci was booked into the Spokane County Jail and was being held on $1 million bond.

The Old Trails Fire was first reported Saturday near North Old Trails Road and West Euclid Road. It became the largest of three destructive fires burning around Spokane and remained uncontained Monday, according to authorities and wire reports.

The three fires had collectively destroyed at least 700 structures and prompted evacuation orders affecting approximately 67,000 people as of Monday, according to The Associated Press. More than 1,000 firefighters were battling the blazes.

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson declared a statewide wildfire emergency Saturday amid drought, unusually high temperatures and strong winds. The declaration also imposed a statewide prohibition on most outdoor and agricultural burning through Sept. 30.

item.title: Pennsylvania school bus aide accused of sexually assaulting special needs teen
item.description: A Pennsylvania bus aide faces indecent assault and child endangerment charges after allegedly inappropriately touching a special needs student.
item.content:encoded:
A Pennsylvania school bus aide was arrested after he allegedly inappropriately touched a 14-year-old girl with special needs and appeared to take photographs and videos of her with his cellphone, according to police.

Ali Khan, 62, was charged with endangering the welfare of a child, corruption of minors, indecent assault and related offenses, the Bensalem Township Police Department said.

Khan was being held at the Bucks County Correctional Facility after failing to post 10% of his $500,000 bail.

The girl’s parents contacted police on Thursday, July 30, to report that their daughter had allegedly been inappropriately touched by a bus aide earlier that day, according to investigators.

HIGH SCHOOL COUNSELOR PLEADS GUILTY TO MULTIPLE SEX CRIMES INVOLVING TEEN SHE WAS MEANT TO HELP

Police said their investigation determined that Khan allegedly touched the Bensalem High School student multiple times on Wednesday, July 29, and Thursday, July 30, while she was riding a bus to the school’s extended school year program.

Investigators said surveillance footage from inside the bus showed Khan directing the girl to a specific seat before allegedly touching her inappropriately while securing her seatbelt and after she was seated. 

Police said the footage also appeared to show Khan engaging in sexual conduct and using a cellphone to photograph or record the girl.

"Bensalem Police would like to commend the victim of this assault for having the courage to come forward and report the assault," police said. "Additionally, Bensalem Police would like to thank the Bensalem School District for their assistance with this investigation. The safety and well-being of our students continues to be the top priority of both the Bensalem Township Police Department and the Bensalem School District."

The Bensalem Township School District said the employee was immediately removed from service and from the district pending the outcome of criminal and administrative investigations.

"The safety and well-being of our students is our highest priority," the district said in a statement. "Whenever concerns involving student safety are brought to our attention, we act immediately to protect students, support families, and cooperate fully with law enforcement. We are committed to conducting a thorough administrative review while respecting the integrity of the criminal investigation."

CALIFORNIA MIDDLE SCHOOL ASSISTANT PRINCIPAL NABBED IN CHILD SEX STING

"The district is fully cooperating with the Bensalem Township Police Department and will continue to assist law enforcement as requested. The district will also continue its own administrative investigation in accordance with Board policy, district procedures, and applicable law," the statement added.

Khan’s preliminary hearing is scheduled for Aug. 11, 2026.

The incident remains under investigation.

item.title: Lindsay Clancy defense scores ‘extremely helpful’ psychosis concession as expert flags next hurdle
item.description: A hospital psychiatrist agreed that Lindsay Clancy could plan and communicate while psychotic, a key concession in the Duxbury murder trial.
item.content:encoded:
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, contact the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

Lindsay Clancy’s attorney sought to blunt prosecutors’ portrayal of the Massachusetts mother as organized and calculating, pressing a hospital psychiatrist to acknowledge that a person can communicate, make plans and carry them out while experiencing psychosis.

"People can communicate and plan and act on plans even if they’re in the middle of a psychosis, right?" defense attorney Kevin Reddington asked Dr. Sejal Shah Monday.

HEATED LINDSAY CLANCY COURTROOM EXCHANGE OVER 911 CALL, CRIME SCENE PHOTOS SETS STAGE FOR MOM’S MURDER TRIAL

"Yes," Shah replied.

Reddington then asked whether someone must be "drooling and stumbling and unable to walk and talk" to be psychotic. Shah said no and agreed that a person in psychosis can still communicate with others.

Clancy is charged in the deaths of Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, inside the family’s Duxbury home. Her defense maintains she was suffering from postpartum psychosis. Prosecutors argue she acted deliberately and understood what she was doing.

LINDSAY CLANCY’S EX-HUSBAND DETAILS ‘BIG SPIRAL’ AS EXPERT SAYS ONE PART ‘SCARED ME’ IN MOM’S MURDER TRIAL

Seth J. Zuckerman, a celebrity criminal defense attorney, former New York City prosecutor and founder of Zuckerman Legal Group, said the case will turn on Clancy’s mental state at the precise time the children were killed.

Shah, an associate chief of psychiatry and medicine at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, first evaluated Clancy five days after the killings.

She testified that Clancy was confused, made mistakes during a cognitive assessment and had experienced visual hallucinations after spinal surgery.

Shah diagnosed delirium and said possible causes included anesthesia, oxygen problems and an elevated heart rate. The symptoms resolved by the following day, Shah said.

During later evaluations, Clancy appeared calm and cooperative, displayed organized and goal-directed thinking and denied hallucinations and suicidal or homicidal intent.

Reddington used cross-examination to argue those observations did not establish Clancy was free of psychosis at the time of the killings.

"Was she, in your opinion and your experience, an honest patient telling you what her symptoms were, if any?" Reddington asked.

Zuckerman called that concession "extremely helpful to the defense," although not decisive.

On redirect, prosecutors challenged the defense’s portrayal by focusing on Clancy’s medication history.

Shah also confirmed that Clancy requested do-not-resuscitate status after surviving her fall from a second-story window. The hospital did not immediately change her status because of the reported suicide attempt.

"The burden is on the prosecutors to show that she was criminally responsible at the time of the deaths," Zuckerman said. "That is unique to Massachusetts, and I think it’s beneficial to the defense here."

item.title: Bears $40M free agent signing gets emotional after knee injury, but diagnosis brings sigh of relief
item.description: Coby Bryant was emotional after being carted off the field during a drill against Cole Kmet, but his knee injury won't end his first Bears season.
item.content:encoded:
Coby Bryant’s Chicago Bears tenure is not off to the start he wished, as he was emotional after being carted off the training camp field during Monday’s practice.

There is a bright side to Bryant’s situation, though, despite needing to miss time.

Bryant was very upset as he got himself onto the cart after suffering a knee injury, expecting the worst just days into his Bears career one season after winning the Super Bowl with the Seattle Seahawks.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Bryant was facing tight end Cole Kmet during a 1-on-1 drill where he went down and immediately clutched at his leg. But Bryant’s injury got a better diagnosis than he initially believed.

It won’t be season-ending for Bryant, as ESPN reported the safety will miss eight-to-10 weeks after suffering a hyperextended knee, bone bruise and small fracture.

PANTHERS DEFENSE TAKES MAJOR HIT AS STAR PASS RUSHER SUFFERS MAJOR INJURY ON FIRST DAY OF CAMP: REPORTS

Bryant signed a three-year, $40 million deal to join the Bears this offseason, bolstering a secondary that was overhauled following multiple departures.

He figured to be a mainstay after proving his worth with the Seahawks during his rookie deal, where he tallied seven interceptions and helped his team win the Super Bowl.

Bryant may not be available during Week 1, but since that’s five weeks away, he shouldn’t be gone for long when the regular season finally kicks off.

"It always sucks to see," second-year tight end Colston Loveland said about Bryant’s injury, per the New York Post. "That’s part of it. You know, he’s tough, he’s a dog. He’s going to be fine."

As Bryant will attack rehab, the Bears’ depth chart will be tested. They spent their first-round draft selection on Oregon standout safety Dillon Thieneman, who was always considered the team’s starting free safety next to Bryant. But Cam Lewis, who was at slot cornerback after Kyler Gordon suffered a previous injury, will likely move to safety to fill the gap there.

Lewis is another free agent signee for the Bears, who lost Kevin Byard, Jaquan Brisker, Nahshon Wright, C.J. Gardner-Johnson and Jonathan Owens this offseason. Lewis spent the past six seasons with the Buffalo Bills.

This is the time of year when teams are hoping for health, but the NFL knows all too well that depth determines just how far a team goes come February.

The Bears are feeling that early on, but they won’t have to go the entire season without a main free agent addition during the 2026 NFL season.

item.title: Tarik Skubal dismisses outrage over joining Los Angeles Dodgers with blunt message to fans
item.description: Tarik Skubal defends the Los Angeles Dodgers after his blockbuster trade deadline acquisition, saying every team had the same chance to get him.
item.content:encoded:
When the Los Angeles Dodgers landed Tarik Skubal at the 2026 trade deadline, baseball's usual chorus fired up on cue: the Dodgers are ruining the sport.

The newest ace in Dodger blue, however, isn't buying it.

Speaking to the media Monday while the Dodgers were on the road, Skubal had a message for everyone: Don't blame Los Angeles for trying to win.

DODGERS REPORTEDLY ACQUIRE ACE TARIK SKUBAL FROM TIGERS IN TRADE THAT STIRS UP MLB WORLD

"Every team could trade for me," Skubal said.

"I don't sympathize with people that blame the Dodgers for anything they've done. It's a winning org... I really don't sympathize with people that are complaining because the Dodgers do all the right things."

Fresh off back-to-back AL Cy Young Awards in 2024 and 2025, the elite left-hander arrives in Los Angeles with a 2.79 ERA and 116 strikeouts through 16 starts this season.

After watching Sunday's game from the Dodger Stadium dugout in his new threads, Skubal is slated to make his Dodgers debut Tuesday at Wrigley Field against the Chicago Cubs. He knows what winning looks like, and he sees nothing wrong with the Dodgers' approach.

Skubal's comments get to the heart of one of baseball's most predictable debates. Every time the Dodgers land another star, the calls for a hard salary cap start all over again. But that's treating a salary cap like a cure for problems it can't actually solve.

Cheering for a salary cap is an odd hill to die on.

MLB'S SALARY CAP PROPOSAL WON'T FIX THE LEAGUE'S NON-EXISTENT COMPETITIVE BALANCE PROBLEMS

Outside of sports, consumers don't root for companies to spend less or workers to earn less. Nobody begs Hollywood studios to cut blockbuster movie budgets so smaller productions have a better shot at the box office. Yet in baseball, fans routinely side with billionaire owners and argue for limits on player salaries in the name of "fairness."

It doesn't hold up.

A salary cap doesn't magically turn struggling franchises into smart ones. It doesn't help them draft better, develop talent, or build winning cultures. What it does is give tight-fisted ownership groups another excuse to cash revenue-sharing checks while avoiding the hard work of building a legitimate contender.

As Skubal pointed out, the Dodgers didn't exploit some secret loophole to land him.

Every other team had the same opportunity. Los Angeles drafted well, developed valuable trade chips and made winning the priority. Baseball should not punish the Dodgers; the rest of the league should try to emulate them, frankly.

Instead of begging MLB to handicap organizational excellence, rival fans should demand more from their own front offices.

item.title: Tennis star Aryna Sabalenka supports WTA transgender rules, says males shouldn't face women
item.description: Aryna Sabalenka backed the WTA's new genetic testing policy in Montreal, saying she'd gladly undergo the screening herself to protect women's tennis.
item.content:encoded:
Tennis World No. 1 Aryna Sabalenka didn't mince words during her Canadian Open press conference in Montreal when asked about the WTA's new transgender eligibility policy.

The Belarusian star threw her support behind the guidelines, which have been criticized by pro-trans activists.

When asked for her thoughts, Sabalenka responded, "I think it's really important to keep the fairness in our tour."

WOMEN'S TENNIS LEGEND SPEAKS OUT ON CALIFORNIA TRANS ATHLETE CONTROVERSY AS NEWSOM FACES CRITICISM

"Biologically, men are way stronger than women, so I feel like it would not really be fair for women to compete against biological men," she added.

She called the measure a fair and necessary step to protect the women's tour, saying the WTA "took them a little while to make this decision" but that she supports the policy.

Addressing the requirement for players to undergo a one-time genetic screening for the SRY gene on the Y chromosome, Sabalenka made her position clear.

"If they want to test us all, I'm happy to do that. It's pretty fair, and let's keep it that way."

After years of agenda-driven sports media, athletes themselves are fed up with administrators dancing around biological reality. Without clear, sex-based boundaries, the entire rationale for a protected women's category completely collapses.

For years, governing bodies dragged their feet, attempting to appease bad-faith critics while female athletes paid the price.

The WTA finally drew a firm line in the sand, anchoring the sport back to a fundamental premise: women’s sports exist specifically because biological sex matters at all levels of competition.

Sabalenka is far from alone in making this stand. Her comments mirror those of 18-time Grand Slam champion Martina Navratilova, who routinely dismantles online outrage over the WTA's protocol. Navratilova silenced the critics with logic: the WTA was created for biological females, and the men's division remains open to any male athlete who wants to play.

MARTINA NAVRATILOVA SAYS BILLIE JEAN KING’S TRANS-ATHLETE STANCE ‘DOESN’T SQUARE’ WITH HER OWN WORDS

From bone density and muscle mass to heart size and lung capacity, male puberty confers undeniable physical advantages that training alone can never bridge.

Protecting the female category isn't about exclusion, it exists for the exact same reason weight classes do: to ensure fair competition.

Step back from the tennis court, and a clear shift is happening across the entire athletic landscape. Fans are starving for athletes who refuse to hide behind PR scripts.

The same dynamic played out earlier this summer when Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham offered a straightforward defense of women's basketball, drawing widespread public support.

When female athletes defend their hard-earned categories without apology, fans respond in droves.

Sabalenka didn't step to the microphone looking to make a political statement. She simply defended the integrity of her sport.

By backing the WTA's policy without hesitation, the world's top player drew a line that should never have been blurred: keeping women's sports female isn't a political debate; it's basic common sense.
